results.result: The manuscript describes three sequential waves of hematopoiesis in mice: primitive hematopoiesis in the yolk sac around E7.5, transient definitive hematopoiesis from erythromyeloid progenitors (EMPs) around E8.5, and definitive hematopoiesis from HSCs around E10.5 in the aorta-gonado-mesonephros region. Early yolk sac EMP-derived macrophages seed tissues between E8.5-E10.5 but are outcompeted by late EMP-derived fetal monocytes from the fetal liver, which colonize organs pre- and perinatally and maintain themselves via endogenous proliferation throughout life. The fetal liver serves as the main hematopoietic hub during development until HSCs move to the bone marrow perinatally.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C34 are well-supported by multiple citations to published research (Palis et al., 1999; McGrath et al., 2015; Boisset et al., 2010; Stremmel et al., 2018; Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015; Hoeffel et al., 2015; Hashimoto et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2012) and are consistent with Figure 1. The temporal sequence and cellular origins are clearly documented in the literature, and the synthesis of these findings into a coherent developmental model is appropriate.

results.result: EMP-derived macrophages persist in specific tissues into adulthood (brain microglia, liver Kupffer cells, epidermis Langerhans cells), while in other specialized niches (dermal macrophages, intestinal lamina propria, brain choroid plexus), macrophages are replaced by HSC-derived progenitors from birth onwards. Each tissue-resident macrophage population carries a transcriptional signature imprinted by hematopoietic origin, and upon entry into anatomical niches, macrophages adapt to the tissue environment through tissue-specific transcriptional programs defined by neighboring cells, metabolites, growth factors, and microbial stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C41 are supported by multiple citations (Gentek et al., 2018a,b; Goldmann et al., 2016; Kolter et al., 2019; Bain et al., 2014; Van Hove et al., 2019; Hagemeyer et al., 2016; Lavin et al., 2014; Mass et al., 2016; van de Laar et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020; Bonnardel et al., 2019; Sakai et al., 2019; Okabe and Medzhitov, 2014; Capucha et al., 2018). The evidence demonstrates tissue-specific patterns of macrophage origin, maintenance, and transcriptional programming.

results.result: During perinatal establishment of definitive hematopoiesis, HSPCs require a supportive bone marrow environment including osteoblasts, endothelial cells, and mesenchymal stem cells. Upon bone marrow egress, immune cells carry developmental programs determined by genetic, epigenetic, and environmental cues. Differentiation of circulating innate immune cells (monocytes, granulocytes) is hierarchical and tightly regulated, with egress controlled by CCR2, CXCR2, CXCR4, and G-CSFR signaling. Monocytes and neutrophils are highly plastic and adaptable to different tissue environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C50 are supported by appropriate citations (Coşkun et al., 2014; Sugiyama et al., 2006; Hooper et al., 2009; Mildner et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019; Semerad et al., 2002; Serbina and Pamer, 2006; Eash et al., 2009; Guilliams et al., 2018; Giladi et al., 2020; Ballesteros et al., 2020; Lösslein et al., 2021). The claims describe well-established mechanisms of hematopoietic stem cell niche biology and immune cell differentiation.

results.result: The perinatal phase is crucial for immune cell maturation and acquisition of immunocompetent phenotypes, including tissue macrophage differentiation and adaptation. Macrophages undergo rapid transcriptional adaptation within their niches, and these differentiation processes maintain both numeric homeostasis and balanced infection responses. Early immune cell dissemination to organs is associated with important lifelong functions, though whether effects later in life are secondary to early tissue seeding or direct cellular persistence remains enigmatic.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are supported by citations (Matcovitch-Natan et al., 2016; Thion et al., 2018; Kolter et al., 2019; Feuerstein et al., 2020; Cossío et al., 2019) and synthesize the importance of the perinatal period. However, C55 appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about mechanisms, which is a strength of the evaluation. The claims are well-grounded in the cited literature.

results.result: Perinatal immune development follows common principles (genetic determination, in utero modulation, postnatal adaptation) but also depends on spatial and temporal signals at distinct body sites. Cellular immune development occurs in parallel with development of other cell types (fibroblasts, endothelial/epithelial cells, neurons), which harbor immunological properties and form cellular niches as discrete working units for tissue immunity. Macrophage renewal patterns relate to tissue substructure, with multicellular networks tightly regulating renewal and density via mechanisms including quorum sensing.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C62 are supported by citations (Guilliams et al., 2020; Kolter et al., 2019; Lohrmann et al., 2021) and provide a conceptual framework for understanding tissue-specific immune development. The integration of immune and non-immune cell development is well-established, and the claims appropriately synthesize this complexity.

results.result: In the skin, nerve-associated macrophages in the dermis and Langerhans cells in the epidermis maintain population size in a microbiota-independent fashion, while other macrophages and Tγδ17 cells are heavily influenced by skin flora. The network of resident immune cells depends on interactions with non-professional immune cells (keratinocytes, fibroblasts). Nerve-associated macrophages are dedicated to microanatomical niches with distinct transcriptomic programs, function in nerve surveillance, and maintain themselves by self-renewal, while nearby macrophages are replaced by HSC-derived progenitors. Upon injury and niche expansion, macrophages of other origins can adopt nerve-niche specific programs.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C73 are well-supported by multiple citations (Capucha et al., 2018; Ridaura et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019a; Di Domizio et al., 2020; Abtin et al., 2014; Barreiro et al., 2016; Goldmann et al., 2016; Kolter et al., 2019; Bain et al., 2014; Van Hove et al., 2019; De Schepper et al., 2018). The claims demonstrate the complexity of skin immune cell populations and their differential regulation by microbiota and tissue microenvironment.

results.result: Epidermal Langerhans cells are functionally positioned between macrophages and dendritic cells and develop from both early yolk sac progenitors and fetal liver monocytes before self-renewing in adults. Starting at E14.5, EMP-derived fetal monocytes enter the developing skin and differentiate to LC progenitors. Shortly before birth, LC progenitors colonize the separating epidermis and differentiate to mature LCs postnatally, losing monocyte markers and acquiring LC markers (Langerin, CD11c, MHC-II). Maturation and maintenance depend on keratinocyte-derived signals including IL-34/Csf1r, though perinatal differentiation signals remain unidentified. LCs are maintained by endogenous proliferation but can be replaced by HSC-derived progenitors after injury (UV-B irradiation).
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C82 are supported by appropriate citations (Gentek et al., 2018a; Merad et al., 2002; Hoeffel et al., 2012; Chorro et al., 2009; Greter et al., 2012; Seré et al., 2012). C81 appropriately identifies a gap in knowledge about perinatal differentiation signals. C83 about γδ T cells is also well-supported (Sandrock et al., 2018). The developmental timeline and cellular mechanisms are clearly documented.

results.result: In the adult lung, local immune defense is provided by tissue-resident macrophages (interstitial and alveolar). In fetal/newborn mice, the lung immune system is established via three waves: (1) YS-derived macrophages from E10 (high F4/80, low CD11b) that remain as interstitial macrophages and are postnatally renewed by bone marrow monocytes; (2) fetal liver-derived monocytes from E12 (low F4/80, high CD11b) that show strong proliferation from E16 and establish alveolar macrophages around birth, outcompeting YS macrophages with lasting consequences for lung function; (3) bone marrow-derived monocytes starting immediately after birth that fill interstitial macrophage niches. Similar mechanisms may apply to human lung development.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C93 are well-supported by multiple citations (Evren et al., 2020; Kopf et al., 2015; Guilliams et al., 2013; Hashimoto et al., 2013; Tan and Krasnow, 2016; Li et al., 2020). The three-wave model of lung macrophage development is clearly documented with specific temporal markers and functional consequences. C93 appropriately notes extension to human development with a recent citation.

results.result: Alveolar macrophages play a central role in immediate postnatal lung protection, exhibiting unique territorial behavior (one AM per three alveoli). Positioning and transition of prealveolar macrophages to AMs requires L-plastin and depends on GM-CSF from alveolar epithelial cells, which activates PPAR-γ to control AM maturation and maintenance. This unique GM-CSF dependence is illustrated by alveolar proteinosis disease. AMs maintain self-renewal capacity throughout life but can be replaced by circulating monocytes after severe damage. Both pulmonary development and immune system establishment are ongoing after birth, making the lung vulnerable to disturbances. In premature infants, noxious agents can lead to bronchopulmonary dysplasia with long-term consequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C105 are supported by appropriate citations (Neupane et al., 2020; Todd et al., 2016; Kopf et al., 2015; Schneider et al., 2014; Trapnell et al., 2019; Epelman et al., 2014; Machiels et al., 2017; Lavin et al., 2014; van de Laar et al., 2016; Blackwell et al., 2011). The molecular mechanisms of AM development and the clinical relevance to premature infants are well-documented.

results.result: Microglia arise from early YS EMPs and colonize the developing brain around E9.5, expanding via endogenous proliferation without input from fetal monocytes or HSC-derived progenitors. With blood-brain barrier establishment around E15.5, the microglial population becomes dependent on self-renewal via proliferation, showing high proliferation prenatally/postnatally but dramatic decline in adults. Microglial maturation involves intrinsic regulators and exogenous cues. Differentiation from EMPs relies on transcription factors Sfpi/Pu.1 and Irf8, with Sfpi/Pu.1-deficient mice lacking microglia and Irf8-deficient mice showing reduced progenitors and maturation defects. Sall1 is a core regulator, with loss abrogating development and causing activation/neurogenesis alterations. Microglial development is highly dependent on CSF1 receptor signaling, with deletion/inhibition resulting in microglia loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C118 are extensively supported by multiple citations (Ginhoux et al., 2010; Kierdorf et al., 2013; Schulz et al., 2012; Hoeffel et al., 2015; Goldmann et al., 2013; Haddad-Tóvolli et al., 2017; Matcovitch-Natan et al., 2016; Thion et al., 2018; Tay et al., 2017; Füger et al., 2017; Hammond et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019; Hagemeyer et al., 2016; Buttgereit et al., 2016; Erblich et al., 2011). The molecular mechanisms and genetic requirements for microglial development are well-established.

results.result: The CSF1 receptor has two ligands (IL-34 and CSF1) expressed in the CNS with spatially distinct patterns that establish postnatally. Gray matter microglia depend predominantly on neuronal IL-34, while white matter microglia depend on astrocyte-derived CSF1, with this pattern emerging around birth. Microglial expansion and homeostasis is highly dependent on TGF-β, with loss causing hyperactivation in adults and impaired expansion during development. Despite residing behind the blood-brain barrier, microglial homeostasis and development are influenced by external cues including gut microbiota. Germ-free mice show maturation defects and altered LPS responses. Microbiota-derived signals highly affect postnatal microglia but less so embryonic microglia. The perinatal phase is important for CNS immune development, with postnatal microglia serving multiple functions and being very dynamic.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C129 are well-supported by citations (Easley-Neal et al., 2019; Kana et al., 2019; Butovsky et al., 2014; Zöller et al., 2018; Utz et al., 2020; Erny et al., 2015; Thion et al., 2018). The spatial and temporal regulation of microglial development by CNS-derived and peripheral signals is clearly documented. The synthesis emphasizing the perinatal phase is appropriate.

results.result: The intestinal mucosa transitions from sterility before birth to dense colonization by commensal bacteria and threat from enteropathogens after birth, with additional dietary antigen exposure upon solid food introduction. Parallel exposure to food and microbiota is beneficial for energy harvesting. The neonatal intestinal mucosa must endure colonization without inflammation, direct beneficial microbiota composition, generate/maintain adaptive immune tolerance to dietary and microbial antigens, and establish antimicrobial reactivity. A timed succession of non-redundant phases facilitates postnatal immune development and mucosal homeostasis establishment. Microbiota-immune interactions have been implicated in various gastrointestinal and extraintestinal disorders, though causal links are not firmly established in all cases.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C136 are supported by citations (Ganal-Vonarburg et al., 2020; Hornef and Torow, 2020; Zheng et al., 2020). The claims appropriately describe the challenges faced by the neonatal intestinal mucosa and acknowledge uncertainty about causal relationships with disease (C136). The conceptual framework is well-grounded in the literature.

results.result: The healthy fetal intestine is sterile, though low levels of maternal microbiota-derived constituents reach the neonate and contribute to immune priming. With amniotic membrane rupture, the neonate contacts maternal vaginal and gastrointestinal bacteria, with maternal fecal bacteria dominant in vaginal delivery and C-section associated with environment/skin-like microbiota. Bacterial density quickly reaches threshold levels, while diversity and stability evolve slowly, influenced by dietary, genetic, environmental, and medical factors. Microbiota buildup follows programmed succession, requiring 2-3 years to reach adult levels in humans. Microbial antigens are present early, while dietary antigens start later with solid food. Neonatal sepsis/meningitis occur early and are important causes of mortality. Specific viruses infect shortly after birth, while most viral infections occur later with increasing contact and cessation of maternal protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C147 are well-supported by multiple citations (de Goffau et al., 2019; Gomez de Agüero et al., 2016; Ganal-Vonarburg et al., 2020; Dominguez-Bello et al., 2010; van Best et al., 2020a,b; Bokulich et al., 2016; van Best et al., 2015; Planer et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2020; Bäckhed et al., 2015; Yatsunenko et al., 2012; Kolter and Henneke, 2017; Ershad et al., 2019; Baasch et al., 2020). The temporal dynamics of microbiota establishment and pathogen exposure are clearly documented.

results.result: Intestinal epithelium and resident immune cells express innate immune receptors (TLRs, NLRs, RIG-I-like helicases) that sense microbial stimuli. Age-dependent receptor expression differences may regulate activation at birth. Shortly after birth, the epithelium undergoes reprogramming to acquire innate immune tolerance via miR-146a-mediated repression of IRAK1, while immune cells are reprogrammed via S100A8/A9-TLR4 interaction. Other regulatory molecules (A20, SIGIRR, IRAK-M, TOLLIP) and factors from neonatal B cells, CD71+ erythroid cells, amniotic fluid, and breast milk contribute to controlling activation. The ability to control inappropriate stimulation depends on gestational age. Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) in preterm infants is thought to result from failure to control microbiota-induced stimulation, with specific causal microorganisms unidentified but proteobacteria alterations likely significant. Probiotic administration modifies microbiota and lowers NEC/sepsis incidence.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C158 are supported by appropriate citations (Pott et al., 2012; Gribar et al., 2009; Lotz et al., 2006; Chassin et al., 2010; Ulas et al., 2017; Vereecke et al., 2010; Nanthakumar et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2007; Elahi et al., 2013; Good et al., 2012; Neu, 2020; Gopalakrishna et al., 2019; van Best et al., 2020b; Panigrahi et al., 2017). C156-C157 appropriately acknowledge gaps in knowledge about NEC causation.

results.result: Maternal fecal bacteria transmission ensures 'successful' microbiota transfer to the next generation. Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) are indigestible complex carbohydrates that foster Bifidobacterium growth. In mice, hepatic bile acid secretion promotes lactobacilli expansion and microbiota maturation. Neonatal gut epithelium TLR5 expression favors non-flagellated bacteria colonization. Despite early lymphocyte homing, the murine adaptive immune system appears actively suppressed during the first two weeks, possibly allowing adaptive immunity establishment while avoiding autoimmunity. Breastfeeding cessation causes microbiota alterations and induces the 'weaning reaction' with transient innate immune stimulation, accelerated fetal macrophage replacement, and adaptive mucosal immunity initiation, propagating regulatory T cell maturation and immune tolerance maintenance. Effector T lymphocytes are then generated for antimicrobial protection. Early T lymphocytes derive from separate progenitors with unique properties (rapid effector responses, reduced memory) matching neonatal requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C170 are supported by citations (Zivkovic et al., 2011; van Best et al., 2020a; Fulde et al., 2018; Torow et al., 2015; Kulkarni et al., 2020; Al Nabhani et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2015; Vatanen et al., 2016; Mold et al., 2010; Rudd, 2020). C159 is an inference about evolutionary advantage, which is reasonable. C164 appropriately presents speculation about immune suppression purpose. The weaning reaction and T cell development are well-documented.

results.result: Infants provide efficient antimicrobial responses despite mucosal immune restrictions through multiple mechanisms: exogenous antimicrobial factors (lactoferrin, antimicrobial peptides, SIgA) in breast milk support pathogen resistance; the neonatal epithelium discriminates between colonization and invasive infection via chemotactic and antimicrobial mediator formation; and newborns mount fast, effective cellular immune responses to viral infection, though emerging T lymphocytes are more prone to rapid effector function than lasting memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C173 are supported by citations (Zhang et al., 2014; Dupont et al., 2016; Pott et al., 2012; Sarzotti et al., 1996). The claims appropriately describe compensatory mechanisms that allow neonatal antimicrobial defense despite developmental limitations.

results.result: Breast milk is a complex cocktail with substantial compositional differences between mothers and over lactation time. Key components (immunoglobulins, cytokines, nutrients, oligosaccharides, microRNAs, hormones, immune cells, microorganisms) are associated with perinatal immune programming. HMOs comprise ~200 bioactive glycans with direct immune effects (antiadhesive, antimicrobial, immune programming), promoting immune cell homeostasis and intestinal barrier integrity. The HMO disialyllacto-N-tetraose concentration is inversely correlated with NEC risk. Limited data suggest HMOs circulate in maternal blood and may cross the placenta, though functional relevance remains to be explored.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C180 are supported by citations (Walsh et al., 2020; Xiao et al., 2019; Šuligoj et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2019b; Masi et al., 2020; Hirschmugl et al., 2019; Wise et al., 2018). C179-C180 appropriately acknowledge limited evidence and gaps in knowledge about placental HMO transfer. The claims about breast milk composition and HMO functions are well-documented.

results.result: HMOs act as prebiotics promoting beneficial bacteria growth that impact mucosal and systemic immunity. HMOs are poorly metabolized by the host but are favored substrates for beneficial Bifidobacterium species. Immune-modulatory effects may occur through recognition of bifidobacterial surface components (exopolysaccharides, tad pili) and production of immune-modulatory metabolites (SCFAs). Increased Bifidobacterium abundance was described during pregnancy in humans and mice, suggesting effects may start before birth via placental crossing of microbial metabolites and in utero programming. However, it remains unclear how specific Bifidobacterium strains and their metabolites trigger immunomodulatory responses maintaining homeostasis during the perinatal period.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C185 are supported by citations (Fulde et al., 2018; Alessandri et al., 2019; Nuriel-Ohayon et al., 2019). C185 appropriately identifies a gap in mechanistic understanding. The prebiotic function of HMOs and their relationship to Bifidobacterium are well-established, though specific mechanisms remain incompletely understood.

results.result: Breast milk and colostrum provide micro- and macronutrients with high immune-modulatory activity (amino acids, lipids, vitamins, trace elements). Specific amino acids (glutamate, glutamine) are essential for immune and tissue development. The second largest nutrient fraction comprises lipids, including long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (arachidonic acid, docosahexaenoic acid) that influence lymphocyte proliferation and cytokine production. Iron (bound to lactoferrin) and zinc are central in perinatal immune development and may act indirectly via gut bacteria growth modulation. Obese or malnourished mothers may lack appropriate balance of immune-modulatory components, impacting perinatal immune programming in infants.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C190 are supported by citations (Dror and Allen, 2018; Samuel et al., 2020). The nutritional components of breast milk and their immunological functions are well-documented. C190 appropriately notes potential impacts of maternal nutritional status.

results.result: Direct transfer of immune cells (T cells, NK cells, macrophages) via breast milk may influence perinatal immune development, though it remains unclear whether intact cells can translocate through the infant's mucosal barrier and populate tissues. Recent work suggests even cellular lysate may represent a mechanism for passive transfer of cellular immunity. Stem-cell-like cells in breast milk have high multilineage potential and can traffic to different body sites including the brain. Their differentiation into neuronal and glial cell types has been demonstrated, but it remains unclear whether they can differentiate into immune cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C191-C195 are supported by citations (Laouar, 2020; Torow et al., 2015; Myles and Datta, 2021; Ninkina et al., 2019), but C192 and C195 appropriately acknowledge significant gaps in knowledge about cellular translocation and differentiation potential. The potential for cellular transfer is documented, but the functional significance and mechanisms remain incompletely understood, warranting an UNCERTAIN evaluation.

results.result: Breast milk contains exosomes enriched in immune-modulating proteins, peptides, and miRNAs that may withstand digestion and promote intestinal epithelial cell growth and mucosal barrier development. Immunoglobulins in breast milk include predominantly SIgA (>90%), followed by SIgM, with IgG mainly in mature milk. SIgA has antimicrobial properties but recent data suggest additional roles in enhancing bacterial colonization and homeostatic immunity. T cell help is required for appropriate affinity maturation to bacterial antigens. Growth factors and cytokines (EGF, TGF-β, S100 proteins) are passed via breast milk and modulate mucosal responses, with transfer influenced by birth mode and gestational age. Preterm infants exhibit lower fecal S100 proteins, leading to gut microbiota changes including Bifidobacteriaceae alterations.
results.evaluation: Claims C196-C202 are supported by citations (Hock et al., 2017; Cacho and Lawrence, 2017; Pabst and Slack, 2020; Kawamoto et al., 2012; Kociszewska-Najman et al., 2020; Willers et al., 2020). The immunological components of breast milk and their functions are well-documented, including the relationship between gestational age and immune factor transfer.

results.result: Breast milk contains microorganisms (Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, low numbers of Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus). Associated immune development influence may occur through bacterial metabolites like SCFAs, which modulate immune cell activity via histone deacetylase inhibition and G protein-coupled receptor activation. Butyrate at breast milk concentrations modulated immune responses in an in vivo food allergy model.
results.evaluation: Claims C203-C205 are supported by citations (Demmelmair et al., 2020; Cortes-Macias et al., 2020; Paparo et al., 2020). The presence of microorganisms in breast milk and the mechanisms by which their metabolites affect immunity are documented.

results.result: The enteric microbiota impacts resident immune cell development and function at mucosal sites and beyond (e.g., CNS). Tissue-resident macrophages seeded in embryonic life are postnatally replaced by bone marrow monocyte-derived macrophages in a tissue-specific fashion, influenced by microbiota acquisition or low-grade infections (e.g., herpes viruses for alveolar macrophages). Comparison of SPF mice with germ-free or antibiotic-treated mice may underestimate microbiota contribution since SPF mice are relatively close to GF mice and distant from mice with more diverse 'natural' flora. The role of microenvironment including microbiota on perinatal development of non-professional immune cells (fibroblasts, epithelial cells) has not been sufficiently considered. The impact of maternal microbiota on the placenta as a fetal immune organ remains largely elusive.
results.evaluation: Claims C206-C211 are supported by citations (Oschwald et al., 2020; Elinav et al., 2011; Lohrmann et al., 2021; Bain et al., 2014; Machiels et al., 2017; Rosshart et al., 2019). C209-C211 appropriately identify methodological limitations and gaps in knowledge. The claims about microbiota influence on immune development are well-grounded, and the acknowledgment of knowledge gaps is appropriate.

results.result: During fetal ontogeny, immune cells populate peripheral organs to prepare for postnatal challenges, with distribution relying on blood circulation. In mouse fetuses, blood circulation onset occurs around E8.5 and is fully established by E10.5. During this time, the first monocytes and neutrophils derived from yolk sac EMPs are released into circulation, later replaced by HSC-derived cells from the fetal liver then bone marrow. While early fetal monocytes seed organs and differentiate into tissue-resident macrophages, the fate and function of early circulating neutrophils are less clear. Several lines of evidence support the hypothesis that circulating neutrophils already provide first-line immune response during fetal life. During fetal life, neutrophils exhibit ontogenetically regulated gain of recruitment efficiency into inflamed vessels.
results.evaluation: Claims C212-C219 are supported by citations (Cacho and Lawrence, 2017; Stremmel et al., 2018; McGrath et al., 2003). C217 appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about early neutrophil fate, while C218 presents a reasonable hypothesis. The temporal sequence of blood circulation establishment and immune cell distribution is well-documented.

results.result: Fetal and postnatal neutrophil development follows a cell-intrinsic functional program that does not seem significantly altered by early postnatal life cues, as shown by analysis of preterm and term infant neutrophils. This indicates the ontogenetic neutrophil program is tuned to adapt to the growing organism's needs within the uterus, providing development room while offering protection against exogenous threats. However, neutrophil adaptation to premature postnatal life is rather limited. Paucity and altered neutrophil activation have been traditionally linked to infection susceptibility and high mortality in newborns, especially preterm infants.
results.evaluation: Claims C220-C223 are supported by citations (Sperandio et al., 2013; Nussbaum et al., 2013; Gessler et al., 1995; Henneke et al., 2003). The cell-intrinsic nature of neutrophil development and its clinical implications for preterm infants are well-documented. C221 is an appropriate inference from the data.

results.result: Induced activation of circulating mononuclear phagocytes (monocytes, dendritic cells) from newborn infants has been subject to detailed analysis. Mononuclear phagocytes from cord blood show robust responses to whole bacteria and purified bacterial effectors for some cytokines (TNFα, IL-6, IL-10) but respond weakly with type I interferons to cytomegalovirus infection. Unique properties of cord blood mononuclear cells compared to young infants in cytokine formation have been confirmed by high-dimensional analysis. However, the functional implications of high activation at baseline and after stimulation around birth remain largely enigmatic.
results.evaluation: Claims C224-C227 are supported by citations (Kollmann et al., 2017; Olin et al., 2018). The characterization of cord blood mononuclear cell responses is well-documented. C227 appropriately acknowledges that functional implications remain unclear, which is a strength of the evaluation.

results.result: Distinct immune cell niches exist in complex tissues and undergo major adaptations during the perinatal period. They can be discriminated by distinct cellular programs. Both systemic regulators and microenvironment-specific signals steer homing and homeostatic maintenance of resident immune cells by transcriptionally redirecting progenitors from different sources. The impact of exogenous signals (establishing microbiota, microbial metabolites) and tissue-intrinsic factors (perinatal oxygen tension changes) on local cell composition, differentiation, immune maturation, and the interplay between local and systemic regulatory mechanisms are largely elusive. Understanding these issues is pivotal since perinatal changes set the stage for tissue adaptation, immune homeostasis, and long-term health, potentially facilitating development of interventional strategies to prevent disease disposition during this critical period.
results.evaluation: Claims C228-C232 provide an appropriate synthesis and conclusion. C231 appropriately identifies major gaps in knowledge about the impact of various signals on immune development. C232 emphasizes the importance of understanding perinatal immune development for potential interventions. These claims are well-grounded in the preceding evidence and appropriately acknowledge both what is known and what remains to be discovered.

results.result: At birth, tissue macrophages originate from three sources that prenatally seed developing body sites in sequential waves. Postnatally, macrophage self-maintenance and renewal by bone marrow-derived monocytes are subject to microanatomical, soluble endogenous and exogenous cues. Establishment of dynamic, tissue-specific macrophage homeostasis relies on tightly regulated late prenatal and early postnatal events.
results.evaluation: Claims C233-C235 are supported by Figure 1 and the extensive discussion in the text. These claims synthesize the major findings about macrophage ontogeny and are well-grounded in the cited literature throughout the manuscript.

results.result: At the transition from intrauterine to postnatal life, drastic alterations are mirrored by changes in cellular immunity. These changes are immune cell intrinsic, originate in fetal cell replacement, or result from global regulatory mechanisms and tissue microenvironment adaptation. Longer developmental trajectories are intersected by events related to mother-infant separation, birth cues, microbiota acquisition, and metabolic factors. Perinatal alterations particularly affect immune niches where structures with discrete functions meet (intestinal mucosa, epidermis, lung). Birth constitutes the end of fetal development, a complex transition, and the beginning of extrauterine life with environmental challenges. The immune system undergoes broad adaptations, and a precisely tuned immune system is key to healthy neonatal life since microorganisms inevitably colonize during and after birth.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C9 provide an appropriate introduction and framing for the manuscript. These are general statements about perinatal immune development that are well-established in the field and set the context for the more detailed findings presented in the manuscript. The claims are conceptually sound and supported by the extensive evidence presented in subsequent sections.

results.result: The postnatal phase is characterized by intimate immunological interaction between mother and infant: immunologically active molecules are transferred via breast milk, bacterial microbiota members are provided by mother to offspring, most systemic immune effectors acquired in utero (e.g., maternal antibodies) slowly wane after birth, yet maternal immune cells may circulate in the infant for a long time (microchimerism).
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 describe well-established aspects of maternal-infant immunological interaction. These are general knowledge claims that are supported by the detailed evidence about breast milk components and microbiota transfer presented later in the manuscript.

results.result: Traditionally, immune system ontogeny has been considered to follow an upward 'maturation' trajectory starting in fetal life, with substantial development in the first months after birth. This model was based on concepts that the fetus is largely spared from microorganisms and exogenous stressors, and the semi-allogenic fetal-maternal state requires fetal 'stealth' characteristics and tight maternal immune control. Immune activation or inflammation in utero has been considered unwanted or harmful, promoted by diseases involving pathological immune activation (e.g., elevated type I interferon signaling from congenital viral infections or Aicardi-Goutières syndrome causing intrauterine growth retardation and fetal demise). However, it has been a conundrum that the fetus needs to be both tolerogenic in utero and prepared to instantly switch to a protective immune program with heightened local activation when microbially colonized at birth.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 appropriately describe the traditional model of immune development and its limitations. C18 is supported by citations (Yockey and Iwasaki, 2018; Yockey et al., 2018). C19 identifies a key paradox that motivates the manuscript's focus on perinatal immune development. These claims provide important historical and conceptual context.

results.result: High complexity in immune development before, during, and after birth manifests in distinct profiles of both activating and dampening inflammatory components at birth (high neutrophils, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, tissue-resident regulatory T and myeloid-derived suppressor cells, high IL-10 and IL-1β). Global regulators (S100A8/A9, type I IFN, PGE-2) tune immunity at the beginning of life. Infections early in life may have long-term effects by altering immune cell composition/state in tissues or bone marrow with lasting effects on stem cell progeny. Infection-driven neonatal CD8+ T cell entry into the brain induces lasting epigenetic changes in microglia impacting hippocampal function and behavior during adolescence. Together, neonatal immunity is not immature but highly regulated and specialized to meet the unique challenges of birth and transition into the animated environment.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C24 are supported by citations (Kollmann et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2019; Ulas et al., 2017; Machiels et al., 2017; Kaufmann et al., 2018). C23 is based on unpublished data from the authors (Schwabenland, Henneke unpublished), which is a limitation but the claim is presented appropriately. C24 provides an important synthesis challenging the traditional 'immaturity' model. These claims are well-grounded in the evidence.
